title: the standing prayer
hookLine: the standing prayer; "sarbat da bhala" — the good of all

cards: End of the service. Someone steps forward, and the whole room rises: palms together, facing the scripture. Plenty of people have stood for it since they were small without knowing what's being said.
Then a voice calls out, bole so nihal, and the room shouts back, sat sri akal. Today, what everyone is standing for.

teach.b: It's the Ardas. The word comes from Persian, for a petition, a humble request. Sikhs say it standing, facing the Guru Granth Sahib, at the end of services and before anything important: a wedding, a journey, a new home.

It has a shape. It opens by remembering the Gurus, one by one, from Nanak on. Then it remembers more: the scripture, the five beloved from yesterday, and the men and women who suffered for their faith.

teach.h: A PRAYER WITH A LONG MEMORY.
teach.b: A prayer with a long memory. Then it turns personal.
The one leading adds the day's requests: a new baby, a grandmother in the hospital, thanks for a new job. So no two are quite the same. And the end never changes.

teach.h: SARBAT DA BHALA — THE GOOD OF ALL.
teach.b: It asks for chardi kala, ever-rising spirits, and then three words: sarbat da bhala. The good of all. Not the good of Sikhs, or of this room.
Everyone. After all that memory, the last thing asked for is the well-being of the whole world. Then comes the shout.
Bole so nihal: whoever says it is blessed. And the answer, sat sri akal: true is the timeless one. The same words many Sikhs use to say hello.

how: Sikhs stand with palms joined, facing the Guru Granth Sahib, while one person leads the Ardas at the end of services and before important events; it closes by asking for chardi kala and sarbat da bhala, the good of all, and the congregation answers the call "bole so nihal" with "sat sri akal."

games.q: what's inside the prayer — tap the pairs.

s: the Ardas is exactly the same every time
the opening and closing are fixed, but the middle carries the day's own requests.
the Ardas ends by asking for the good of everyone
sarbat da bhala: not only Sikhs, not only the room.
Sikhs say the Ardas sitting down
it's the standing prayer: the congregation rises, palms joined.

games.q: you're closing a prayer that has just remembered centuries of your community's suffering. what do you ask for last?
o: justice against those who caused it.
the good of all, everyone, everywhere.
games.why: the Ardas ends with sarbat da bhala: the good of all. after all that memory, the last request is for the whole world.

p: remembering the five and the martyrs

practice: Three breaths with the bell. Stand if you can, palms together. On the first, bring to mind the people closest to you.
On the second, widen it to strangers. On the third, widen it once more, to someone you find hard to wish well.

wordCard.voice: Ardas. The standing prayer: it remembers, it asks, and it ends by asking for the good of all. Fifth word.

orig.note: Punjabi, in Gurmukhi script: ardas, a petition or humble request; from Persian.

carryVoice: Your line: for everyone, not just us. Those are the prayer's last words, and they leave nobody out. Day five, done.

sources.ref: Ardas, as set out in the Sikh Rehat Maryada (including the closing 'Nanak naam chardi kala, tere bhane sarbat da bhala')
Var Sri Bhagauti Ji (opening of the Ardas), attributed to Guru Gobind Singh
the jaikara 'bole so nihal, sat sri akal' after the Ardas
